title: Diff
summary: git diff shows exactly which lines changed: removed lines start with -, added lines with +.

levels.title: Spot the change
levels.briefing: git diff compares your files with what is staged. Lines starting with - were removed and lines starting with + were added. git diff --staged compares what is staged with the last commit.
levels.objective: One line in poem.txt was changed. Write the old version of that line into old.txt and commit only old.txt.

cheatsheet.description: Changes staged for the next commit

files.poem.txt:
Roses are red
Violets are blue
Git is great
And so are you

all.content:
Roses are red
Violets are blue
Git is great
And so are you

hints: In git diff, the old line starts with -.
The old line is "Git is great". Do not stage poem.txt.
Run: echo "Git is great" > old.txt, git add old.txt, git commit -m "Save old line"
levels.successMessage: The - line in the diff was the old version, and poem.txt's change is still unstaged.

levels.title: Staged changes
levels.objective: A change to list.txt is already staged. Find the item it added, write it into item.txt, and commit everything.
hints: Plain git diff shows nothing, because the change is staged.
git diff --staged shows the added line.
Run: echo bread > item.txt, git add item.txt, git commit -m "Add bread"
levels.successMessage: git diff --staged shows exactly what your next commit will contain.

levels.title: The removed line
levels.objective: Two files changed. Stage only the file where a line was removed.
hints: Removed lines start with - in the diff.
levels.successMessage: Reading the diff before staging helps you commit exactly what you meant to.

levels.title: The new word
levels.objective: One word in greeting.txt changed. Write the new word into word.txt, then commit both files.
hints: Compare the - line and the + line.
Run: echo there > word.txt, git add ., git commit -m "New greeting"
levels.successMessage: A diff shows whole lines, so a one-word change appears as one line removed and one added.
